analysis.one_liner: Weakens state water-quality reviews and environmental rules to speed permits for pipelines, LNG plants, and nuclear reactors.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate on April 30, 2026, with no cosponsors, and was referred to the Environment and Public Works Committee, where it has received no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the federal permitting rules that apply to major energy projects. It would sharply limit states' power to block or condition pipelines and other projects that discharge into rivers and wetlands, bar FERC from weighing environmental factors when approving LNG terminals, make it easier and cheaper to get general permits for pipeline and dredging work, extend nuclear reactor licenses to 60 years and exempt some new reactors from environmental review, and make it much harder to sue over environmental reviews — including a provision barring nearly all review of decisions affecting tribal trust lands. The bill has one Republican sponsor, no cosponsors, and sits in committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies building oil and gas pipelines, LNG export terminals, and nuclear reactors, along with other large energy developers whose projects currently face state water-quality certifications, multi-year environmental reviews, and litigation. The bill caps state review at one year, requires states to prove with 'clear and convincing evidence' that no project modification could protect water quality before denying a permit, voids conditions that are not the 'least burdensome' option for the applicant, and orders courts not to vacate flawed environmental reviews — all of which reduce the time, cost, and legal risk that developers face.

how_it_helps.text: The bill limits state water-quality certification under Clean Water Act section 401 to the narrow question of whether a discharge meets water quality standards, caps the state review period at one year with no pausing, treats silence as a waiver, and requires 'clear and convincing evidence' before a state can deny a certification or impose a condition.

It requires the Army Corps of Engineers to maintain a nationwide permit for oil and gas pipelines (nationwide permit 12), doubles the term of general permits from five to ten years, deems fills under three acres a 'minimal' impact that may be permitted without individual review, and ratifies all currently issued general permits as causing no more than minimal cumulative effects.
It adds a subsection to the Natural Gas Act stating that FERC 'may not consider any environmental factors' under NEPA when making LNG public-interest findings.

It extends commercial nuclear reactor licenses to up to 60 years, makes early site permits effectively permanent, revocable only on clear-and-convincing evidence of new site-safety information, and categorically excludes new reactors at previously permitted sites from NEPA review.

It limits NEPA lawsuits: claims must be filed within 150 days, by parties who commented and who suffer direct harm; courts may only remand — not vacate or enjoin — noncompliant agency actions, which remain in effect during the 180-day fix-it period; and for actions affecting tribal trust resources, review is barred entirely except for suits brought by the affected tribe itself.

analysis.who_pays: People living near pipelines, LNG terminals, wetlands, and rivers — whose water quality, spill and flood risks, and local say over projects would be reduced — along with state agencies stripped of much of their Clean Water Act certification authority, and federally recognized tribes, who would lose the ability to challenge decisions affecting their trust lands in court (though the tribes themselves retain standing to sue). Taxpayers also bear the cost of shortened federal review periods that may produce more cursory environmental analysis.
analysis.who_pays_short: River and wetland communities, states, and tribes

drawbacks.text: The bill bars courts from vacating or enjoining an agency action found to violate NEPA; the flawed approval stays in effect while the agency has up to 180 days to correct it, meaning a project can proceed or keep operating despite a legally deficient environmental review.

Requiring states to prove by 'clear and convincing evidence' that no modification could avoid a water quality violation — and voiding conditions that are not the 'least burdensome' for the developer — sets a far higher bar than current law, where states may deny or condition certifications based on water quality concerns.

The bill exempts the reissuance of nationwide dredge-and-fill permits from Endangered Species Act consultation and requires only a nationwide environmental assessment, and it treats any fill into fewer than three acres of waters as a 'minimal adverse environmental effect' that may be permitted without individualized review.

A fair-minded objection in its favor: current permitting can take many years and drive up costs for infrastructure of all kinds, including transmission lines and grid improvements; supporters would argue shorter, predictable timelines and concentrated appellate review with deadlines serve builders and ratepayers alike. But the bill's judicial-review limits and no-vacatur rule apply to all NEPA claims, not only ones that fix genuinely procedural delay.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The speed and certainty the bill offers developers is real, and a faster permitting process could benefit some infrastructure projects people rely on. But the bill reaches well beyond delay reduction: it strips states of meaningful leverage over discharges into their waters, bars environmental considerations from LNG approvals, eliminates court-ordered pauses even for reviews a court finds unlawful, and closes the courthouse to almost everyone but the affected tribe for tribal trust land decisions. The costs fall on water quality, communities near projects, and the accountability of federal reviews — costs the public would bear permanently and the industry would not.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee in late April 2026 and has not moved since; no committee vote or floor action has occurred.

narrative.text: Senator David McCormick of Pennsylvania introduced the bill on April 30, 2026, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.
No senators have cosponsored the bill.
No further action, committee markup, or vote has been recorded since the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained yet: the bill has not advanced beyond committee referral, so current permitting law and state certification authority remain unchanged while the bill sits pending.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No change yet; bill sits in committee

for.role: U.S. Senator from Pennsylvania; bill sponsor

sides.party_line_note: No votes have been taken; the bill has a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors, so no partisan pattern is visible in the record.

industries.note: The bill mandates a nationwide permit for oil and gas pipeline construction, ratifies existing general permits as having minimal cumulative impact, caps state review at one year, and sets near-prohibitive standards for state denials. It lowers the cost and legal risk of building pipelines, with water quality and spill exposure falling on nearby communities.

The bill bars FERC from considering any environmental factors under NEPA when making LNG public-interest findings, removing the main avenue communities and agencies have had to weigh air, water, and safety impacts of export terminals.

The bill extends reactor licenses to 60 years, makes early site permits effectively permanent, and exempts new reactors at previously reviewed sites from NEPA. Lower-carbon electricity is a public benefit, but it comes with weakened site review and 60-year license terms issued with limited ongoing environmental scrutiny.

General permits for dredge and fill last twice as long, fills under three acres are deemed minimal-impact, and projects are treated crossing-by-crossing, making it cheaper to build roads, pads, and utility crossings in wetlands. Wetland loss is spread across many small projects the bill treats as negligible.

States lose most of their authority to deny or condition certifications of projects discharging into their waters, with a one-year unpausable clock, a clear-and-convincing denial standard, and federal agencies empowered to void conditions they judge untimely. These agencies exist to protect public waters, so their loss runs against the communities they serve.

Short filing deadlines, comment-based standing requirements, a no-vacatur remedy, and a near-total bar on review of tribal trust decisions sharply reduce these groups' ability to challenge project approvals in court. They are the main channel through which affected residents contest environmental reviews.

analysis.trajectory: With one sponsor, zero cosponsors, and no committee action months after introduction, the bill is unlikely to reach the Senate floor on its own. Permitting provisions like these have a better chance of advancing if folded into a larger must-pass bill such as an energy or funding package, but as a standalone measure it appears headed for the same fate as most single-sponsor bills: no vote before the Congress ends in January 2027.
